newsitem.title: USA: Stocks end mixed in indecisive trading.
newsitem.headline: Stocks end mixed in indecisive trading.

text.p: Stocks ended mixed Monday as investors awaited earnings from IBM and congressional testimony from Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan.

The Dow Jones industrial average rose 16.26 points to 7,906.72, stabilising after Friday's 130-point drop. But declining issues swamped advances, 1,910 to 950, on the New York Stock Exchange, where volume was moderate at 459 million shares.
"I think people are kind of resting before the next wave," said James Volk, director of trading at Jensen Securities.
More profit taking, especially in technology stocks, clipped the tech-heavy Nasdaq composite index, which fell 11.76 to 1,536.23.

But many investors appeared to be awaiting results from International Business Machines Corp., which reported after the market closed that it earned $1.4 billion, or $1.46 a share, in the second quarter, up from $1.3 billion, or $1.26 a share, a year earlier.
Traders said the computer maker's results, which were in line with analysts' estimates of $1.42 a share, according to First Call, could help sooth some recent investor nervousness.
"I don't think there's any shock here either way," said Guy Truicko, equity portfolio manger at Unity Management. "But the fact is that they beat the number."

On Tuesday, Wall Street will be weighing comments from Greenspan on the direction of the economy, interest rates or the stock market itself. The central bank chairman will deliver his semi-annual testimony to Congress on Tuesday and Wednesday.
Analysts said they expect the Fed chief to say the central bank needs to be wary of inflation, despite recent economic data showing muted price rises.
"The market will likely be on hold on the downside until we get through Greenspan," said Richard Cripps, chief market strategist at Legg Mason Wood Walker.
Given the market's sharp gain so far this year, unexpected news coming from Greenspan or elsewhere could trigger a fresh wave of selling, analysts said.
"I think we're vulnerable to a correction, so any kind of bad news is probably going to be very negative for the market," said John Church, chief investment officer at Glenmede Trust Co.
Among other issues, First Union Corp. said it will acquire Signet Banking Corp. for $3.2 billion in stock and Signet jumped 13-8/16 to 50-3/16 while First Union fell 3 to 94-7/16.
The day saw quarterly earnings reports from several stocks in the 30-share Dow.
AT&T Corp. ended off 1/8 to 34-1/4 after it reported a 36 percent drop in profits that were slightly above expectations.
Exxon Corp. beat even the most optimistic forecasts with its quarterly earnings, and its stock rose 14/16 to 61-5/16. Boeing fell 1-11/16 to 54-3/8 after reporting earnings below expectations.
Elsewhere, Kimberly-Clark Corp. fell 4-5/16 to 47-5/16 after reporting slightly lower second quarter earnings, saying results were hurt by Scott Paper operations, which it acquired in 1995.
The Standard & Poor's composite index of 500 stocks fell 2.36 points to 912.94. The American Stock Exchange index was off 3.19 to 630.40.
The NYSE Composite index of all listed common stocks fell 1.47 to 474.50. The average share was down 14 cents.
The Wilshire Associates Equity Index -- the market value of NYSE, American and Nasdaq issues -- was 8,667.273 down 30.506 or 0.35 percent.
